name: Sivalokanathar Temple, Tirupunkur
deity: Shiva as Sivalokanathar, with the goddess Sokkanayaki (Soundaranayaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kaveri delta, sung in the Tevaram (7th century) by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar; the present structure is later, with Chola-era renovation reported
dynasty: Medieval patrons of the Chola country (Chola-era renovation reported, not firmly sourced)
summary: Sivalokanathar is the temple where, tradition says, the great stone Nandi stepped aside so that the humble devotee Nandanar could see the Lord; sung by all three Tevaram saints, it stands among the fields near Vaitheeswaran Koil.

sections.history: Tirupunkur lies among green paddy fields in Mayiladuthurai district, a few kilometres west of Vaitheeswaran Koil. All three great saints of the Tevaram, Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, sang hymns here, which gives it a place of particular honour among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the northern bank of the Kaveri. Its Lord is Sivalokanathar, the Lord of the world of Shiva, believed to have risen of himself from an anthill. A local tradition recalls that Sundarar, visiting in a season of drought, helped a king pray for rain; the rain came so abundantly that the saint was asked to hold it back, and a grant of twenty-four veli of land was then made to the temple. Renovation in the Chola age is reported, though the dates are not firmly known.
sections.architecture: A five-tiered rajagopuram marks the entrance, and the temple opens into a series of quiet enclosures. The Lord is a swayambhu linga, and the goddess Sokkanayaki is honoured in her own shrine on the left side of the temple, with a circumambulatory path of her own. Both the great outer Nandi and the small Nandi in the inner prakaram sit out of line with the sanctum, and the sacred bull is said to be shown with its tongue held within its mouth, unlike the Nandi of most Shiva temples. Within the precincts are shrines to Vinayaka, Subramanya and Surya and a rare panchamukha linga, and the temple tank, the Rishabha Theertham, lies close by.
sections.legends: The great story of Tirupunkur is that of Nandanar, one of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints. Born to humble labouring people and barred by the custom of his age from entering a temple, he loved Shiva with a burning devotion and longed to worship at Tirupunkur. Standing at the outer gate, he could see only the broad back of the stone Nandi that sat directly before the sanctum, hiding the Lord from his sight. In his sorrow he sang to Shiva, and the Lord bade Nandi to move aside. The bull shifted, the linga stood revealed, and Nandanar beheld the Lord face to face. The Nandi remains off-axis to this day. The temple tank is linked to him too, for he is said to have tended the sacred ground and dug the pool; another tradition says that Vinayaka dug it overnight, and Vinayaka is honoured here as Kinaru Vettiya Vinayakar, the Vinayaka who dug the well.
sections.festivals: A ten-day Brahmotsavam at Vaikasi Visakam in May or June is reported as the temple's major festival. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and Nandanar is remembered among the Nayanmar saints in the processions of the Tamil calendar. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Visit Tirupunkur for the Nandi. Stand at the threshold, where Nandanar stood, and notice how the great bull has turned aside to leave the sanctum open to every eye. The setting is simple and rural, with fields all around and a few visitors at any hour. Devotees pause at the tank, at the shrine of the goddess Sokkanayaki, and before the Vinayaka who dug the well. Many come with the thought that devotion, not birth, opens the door to the Lord, which is the lesson this small village keeps for pilgrims from every community.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the early evening, with a long midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally tolerated in the outer prakaram but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple custom. Ask the priest or temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirupunkur lies about 5 km west of Vaitheeswaran Koil, which has a railway station and is the usual base for visiting; Sirkazhi and Mayiladuthurai are nearby railway towns. Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are the main airports. Local buses serve Vaitheeswaran Koil, and an auto-rickshaw or taxi from there is the easiest way to reach the village.
